Name: Betta fish
Note: Long fins need gentle flow and tank mates that neither nip nor resemble a rival betta.

Name: Freshwater angelfish
Note: Tall adults establish territories and may regard very small tetras or fry as prey.

Name: Guppy
Note: Hard-water livebearers breed readily; plan for fry or keep a single-sex group.

Name: Endler's livebearer
Note: Small but constantly active; males show best colour in a planted hard-water aquarium.

Name: Platy
Note: A social livebearer that prefers mineral-rich water and produces frequent broods.

Name: Molly
Note: Mollies need stable, mineral-rich water and more swimming room than their shop size suggests.

Name: Swordtail
Note: Powerful swimmers and persistent males make tank length and a female-biased group important.

Name: Neon tetra
Note: A proper shoal and subdued planting reduce stress; avoid large predatory centrepiece fish.

Name: Cardinal tetra
Note: Warm, soft water and a large shoal suit this Amazonian tetra better than a sparse mixed tank.

Name: Ember tetra
Note: Tiny and gentle; keep a generous group with similarly calm nano species.

Name: Rummy-nose tetra
Note: Tight schooling behaviour needs long open water and excellent, stable water quality.

Name: Glowlight tetra
Note: Dark substrate and a group of eight or more bring out confident colour and movement.

Name: Black skirt tetra
Note: A larger school disperses fin-nipping, but long-finned companions remain a poor choice.

Name: Black neon tetra
Note: A mature planted aquarium, open swimming room and a group of eight or more suit this distinct species—not a black form of the neon tetra.

Name: Lemon tetra
Note: A broad group, subdued cover and clean stable water help the translucent yellow colour and red eye show clearly.

Name: Serpae tetra
Note: Keep a large group to spread chasing, and exclude slow or long-finned companions that invite persistent nipping.

Name: Congo tetra
Note: A long aquarium, a substantial shoal and calm companions protect the species' flowing fins and confident movement.

Name: Harlequin rasbora
Note: A reliable community shoaler that benefits from shaded planting and a broad group.

Name: Chili rasbora
Note: Its minute size calls for mature nano tanks, gentle filtration and no predatory tank mates.

Name: Celestial pearl danio
Note: Dense plants and more females than males reduce sparring and draw this shy fish into view.

Name: Zebra danio
Note: Fast, cool-water swimming and playful chasing can unsettle slow or long-finned fish.

Name: Pearl danio
Note: A long aquarium and a substantial school are more important than extra height.

Name: White cloud mountain minnow
Note: This subtropical shoaler is often kept too warm; avoid permanently tropical temperatures.

Name: Cherry barb
Note: A planted tank and a mixed-sex group bring calmer behaviour and richer male colour.

Name: Tiger barb
Note: Keep a large group to spread aggression and exclude slow, timid and long-finned tank mates.

Name: Rosy barb
Note: A robust subtropical barb needing a long tank and cooler water than many tropical communities.

Name: Gold barb
Note: Best in a well-planted, cooler community with open space for a lively school.

Name: Bronze corydoras
Note: A group on fine, clean substrate can forage naturally without damaging sensitive barbels.

Name: Panda corydoras
Note: Cooler water, good oxygenation and a group of six or more are central to long-term care.

Name: Pygmy corydoras
Note: Unlike larger corys this tiny species also hovers midwater; small peaceful companions are essential.

Name: Peppered corydoras
Note: This cooler-water cory needs a group, clean soft substrate and well-oxygenated water rather than permanently high tropical temperatures.

Name: Sterbai corydoras
Note: One of the warmer-water Corydoras, but it still needs a group of six or more, fine substrate and reliable oxygenation.

Name: Kuhli loach
Note: A soft substrate, many tight hides and a social group help these nocturnal loaches emerge.

Name: Yoyo loach
Note: Social hierarchy, adult size and high activity make a group in a long tank mandatory.

Name: Clown loach
Note: Often sold small, this long-lived giant needs a very large aquarium and a proper group.

Name: Hillstream loach
Note: High dissolved oxygen, strong flow and mature biofilm matter more than a conventional tropical setup.

Name: Bristlenose pleco
Note: Provide real wood, caves and a varied diet; algae alone is neither enough food nor a clean-up plan.

Name: Common pleco
Note: The common name covers very large loricariids that quickly outgrow ordinary home aquariums.

Name: Otocinclus catfish
Note: Add only to a mature aquarium with natural biofilm and supplement its specialised grazing diet.

Name: Pictus catfish
Note: A fast nocturnal predator able to swallow small companions; allow long unobstructed swimming space.

Name: Siamese algae eater
Note: Trade names are unreliable: confirm the unbroken black stripe and clear fins, then provide a long, oxygen-rich aquarium and a proper diet beyond algae.

Name: Flying fox
Note: Often confused with the Siamese algae eater, this territorial adult is best kept singly with ample floor space, current and visual barriers.

Name: Dwarf gourami
Note: Choose healthy stock, provide surface cover and avoid combining multiple males in cramped quarters.

Name: Honey gourami
Note: Gentle companions, floating cover and calm flow suit this shy labyrinth fish.

Name: Pearl gourami
Note: A calm, planted tank with open surface access suits adults better than a boisterous community.

Name: Boesemani rainbowfish
Note: This endangered-in-the-wild shoaler needs hard alkaline water, a long open swimming lane and responsibly sourced captive-bred stock.

Name: German blue ram
Note: Sustained warmth and exceptionally clean, stable water narrow the list of appropriate companions.

Name: Bolivian ram
Note: A comparatively robust dwarf cichlid, though pairs still defend a spawning patch.

Name: Apistogramma group
Note: This is a genus-level overview: exact water, social and harem needs differ substantially by species.

Name: Discus
Note: Large groups, high temperature and very clean water make discus a specialist commitment.

Name: Oscar
Note: Powerful, messy and predatory, an oscar needs robust filtration and carefully selected large companions.

Name: Electric blue acara
Note: Usually measured for a cichlid, but breeding pairs defend territory and can eat small fish.

Name: Convict cichlid
Note: Easy breeding produces intense territorial defence; community plans frequently fail around a pair.

Name: Firemouth cichlid
Note: Allow floor territory and visual barriers; threats intensify sharply during spawning.

Name: Kribensis
Note: A bonded pair can defend a large cave territory, so peaceful behaviour outside spawning is not a guarantee of community safety.

Name: Jack Dempsey cichlid
Note: A large territorial cichlid requiring sturdy decor, space and equally robust companions.

Name: Green terror cichlid
Note: Adult males become large and forceful; generous footprint matters more than decorative tank volume.

Name: Rainbow shark
Note: Keep one per normal aquarium and avoid similar-shaped bottom fish competing for the same space.

Name: Red tail shark
Note: This endangered-in-the-wild cyprinid becomes highly territorial as it matures.

Name: Bala shark
Note: A nervous, very large schooling fish unsuitable for all but exceptional home aquariums.

Name: Senegal bichir
Note: A secure lid is essential; any tank mate that fits in its mouth should be considered prey.

Name: Pea puffer
Note: Tiny size hides specialised feeding and territorial behaviour; species-focused setups are safest.

Name: Common goldfish
Note: A large, active cold-water fish with heavy waste production and a potential lifespan of decades.

Name: Fancy goldfish
Note: Rounded fancy varieties are slower and should not compete with streamlined common goldfish.

Name: African dwarf frog
Note: A fully aquatic air-breather that feeds slowly; deep tanks and fast fish can prevent it reaching food.

Name: Axolotl
Note: Cold water, low flow and species-only care prevent heat stress, gill damage and accidental ingestion.

Name: Cherry shrimp
Note: Mature biofilm and stable minerals support moulting; almost any fish may take shrimplets.

Name: Amano shrimp
Note: An effective grazer but not an algae solution; larvae require brackish development.

Name: Ghost shrimp
Note: The trade name covers several transparent shrimp, so correct identification matters.

Name: Nerite snail
Note: Excellent hard-surface grazers that need minerals; white eggs may be laid but do not hatch in freshwater.

Name: Mystery snail
Note: Leave a safe air gap for egg laying and avoid copper exposure or shell-eroding soft acidic water.

Name: Assassin snail
Note: A snail-eating species, so it is incompatible with ornamental snails the keeper wants to retain.

Name: Rabbit snail
Note: Warm, alkaline water and a mature food supply support its slow growth and reproduction.

Name: Dwarf Mexican crayfish
Note: Even dwarf crayfish can catch resting fish or shrimp; numerous hides reduce but do not remove risk.

Name: Bamboo shrimp
Note: Needs suspended microfoods delivered by clean, directed current and elevated feeding perches.
